The `title:` field names the real upstream Apache Hadoop JIRA / git commit. Your job is to reproduce that upstream change as faithfully as you can from the requirement text plus the code you find in the tree. Hidden tests derived from the real upstream commit will grade the result, so EXACT naming matters:

  * log message wording and format placeholders
  * behavioural details (return values, exception types, ordering, off-by-one boundaries)
If the requirement text names an identifier (class, method, config key, metric, constant), use that identifier verbatim.

HOW TO WORK
1. Read the requirement yaml. Note the JIRA id and the module it belongs to (HDFS / YARN / MAPREDUCE / HADOOP-common / tools).
2. Locate the real code with Grep/Glob. Read enough surrounding code (and the existing tests for it) to make a correct, idiomatic change.
3. Implement the change. Match the surrounding code style, license headers, checkstyle habits (2-space indent, 80-col-ish, final where used, LOG placeholders `{}`).
4. If the change adds a config key, also add it to the matching `*-default.xml` (hdfs-default.xml / core-default.xml / yarn-default.xml / mapred-default.xml) with a sensible description, and to the `DFSConfigKeys`/`YarnConfiguration`/etc. constants class the module uses. Some modules have a TestYarnConfigurationFields / TestHdfsConfigFields style test that requires the xml and the constant to agree - keep them in sync.
5. If the upstream change would have come with tests, add or extend the corresponding test class under the same module (src/test/java/...). Keep tests deterministic and cheap. Do not add tests that need network or a real cluster beyond the usual MiniDFSCluster/MiniYARNCluster idioms already used in that test file.
6. Do NOT run maven/mvn or cmake (there is no warm build environment; it wastes your time). Instead be rigorous by inspection: every symbol you reference must exist (grep to confirm), every new import must be needed and correct, braces/parens balanced, no stale references left behind. Re-read your own final diff (`git diff -- <your files>`) before finishing and fix anything sloppy.
7. Scope discipline: change ONLY what this requirement needs. Do not reformat unrelated lines, do not fix unrelated warnings, do not touch other subsystems. Other agents are concurrently implementing ~380 other requirements in this same working tree.

FORBIDDEN COMMANDS (they would destroy other agents' concurrent work): git checkout / switch / stash / reset / revert / clean / rebase / merge / cherry-pick, `git add -A` or `git add .` without an explicit pathspec, `git commit --amend`, `git rm` of files you did not create, and any `mvn`/`gradle` invocation.

WHEN YOUR IMPLEMENTATION IS COMPLETE - commit it yourself with exactly this shape (substitute the real repo-relative paths you touched, space separated, and keep the flock):

  cd /workspace && flock /tmp/hadoop-git.lock bash -c 'git add -A -- PATH1 PATH2 ... && git diff --cached --binary > requirement_patches/s3a-audit-threadlocal-leak.diff && git commit -q -m "impl: s3a-audit-threadlocal-leak" && git log --oneline -1 && wc -c requirement_patches/s3a-audit-threadlocal-leak.diff'

Rules for that step:
  * List every file you created, modified or deleted as an explicit pathspec. Never a bare directory like `.`.
  * requirement_patches/s3a-audit-threadlocal-leak.diff MUST come out non-empty (wc -c > 0). If `git commit` reports "nothing to commit", another agent already committed your lines: verify the requirement is genuinely satisfied in the working tree, then report that in your notes.
  * Do not touch requirement_patches/ for any other slug.

FINALLY return ONLY a JSON object (this is your return value, not a message to a human):

1	title: HADOOP-18091. S3A auditing leaks memory through ThreadLocal references
2	category: other
3	requirement: "HADOOP-18091. S3A auditing leaks memory through ThreadLocal references

Adds a new map type WeakReferenceMap, which stores weak references to values,
and a WeakReferenceThreadMap subclass to more closely resemble a thread local
type, as it is a map of thread id to value.

construct it with a factory method and optional callback
for notification on loss and regeneration.
```
 WeakReferenceThreadMap<WrappingAuditSpan> activeSpan =
    new WeakReferenceThreadMap<>(
        (k) -> getUnbondedSpan(),
        this::noteSpanReferenceLost);
```
This is used in ActiveAuditManagerS3A for span tracking.

If a calling method has a reference to the span then even with gc the reference will
be valid, it's only if no more references are held that there will be problems.

This does mean that if S3 a code keeps references around then back references to the auditor are retained.

but those classes which can get returned and which do have spans (list iterators, input and\
4	  \ output streams, ...)
And all have callbacks into the main S3a file system anyway. 

Testing this has been fun; about as hard as the production code.

The good news: We can do this in a unit test relatively quickly.
We just create a sequence of audit managers and in each one
Schedule tasks across a thread pool to create spans.
By providing an auditor implementation whose class and spans use lots of memory
We can trigger OOM fast on the original code.

With the new structure this doesn't happen. Instead, and after 100+ iterations
GC calls trigger removal of the only-weakly-referenced spans.

I have run the Itest suites against s3 london and all is well; retesting.

my system is set to fail if any operation is ever executed out of a span, other than those which happened during copy operations when the S3 SDK transfer manager invokes them.

That is the sole risk I can see in this world: that if and external reference is not held then the thread reference will be discarded\
5	  \ prematurely.

I don't see it happening in this case but will review carefully
"

input.new_string:
* Uses a {@link WeakReferenceThreadMap} to store the active span
 * of each thread, rather than a {@code ThreadLocal} reference.
 * This means that the spans -and hence the audit manager and
 * filesystem instances they refer to- are not retained by
 * long-lived threads once all other references to a span have been
 * released (HADOOP-18091).
 * The cost of this is that if garbage collection takes place before
 * a thread switches to a new span, the reference is lost; the
 * unbonded span is then handed back and the auditor notified through
 * {@code OperationAuditor.noteSpanReferenceLost()}.
 */
